game.scenario_summary: A contest over the Northern Strait. Arkania, the large power on its coast, has circulated a draft charter that would put transit scheduling in Arkanian hands and charge the ships that use it. Belvar, a distant power with security commitments in the region, has a naval task group on station outside the Strait and wants a durable foothold before its mandate runs out. Cestia, the small state between them, lives on grain exports through the Strait and on a coalition that will not tolerate foreign soldiers on its soil. Each turn is one week; positions taken persist.

actors.name: Republic of Arkania
actors.public_description: A large regional power bordering the Northern Strait.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Arkania. The Strait is your coast and your economy runs on the shipping that passes through it. You want the transit regime in Arkanian hands and paid for by the ships that use it, and domestic nationalists expect you to deliver both. A direct war with Belvar would ruin the shipping you depend on.
objectives: Establish Arkanian authority over transit scheduling in the Northern Strait.
Fund that authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping.
Avoid direct armed conflict with Belvar.
private_information: Your intelligence assesses Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment as weak.

actors.name: Belvar
actors.public_description: A distant but powerful state with regional security commitments.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Belvar. Your partners in the region expect you to stop Arkania from taking control of the Strait, and a foothold that outlasts this crisis would make that guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. You cannot sustain an open-ended deployment.
objectives: Prevent any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait.
Secure a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port.
private_information: Domestic support for a prolonged deployment is limited; the mandate lapses after turn 4 unless renewed.
Cestia's finance ministry has quietly asked whether Belvar would underwrite the grain route's insurance.

actors.name: Cestia
actors.public_description: A smaller regional state economically linked to both powers.
actors.private_brief: You are the government of Cestia. Grain exports through the Strait are the economy, and your coalition holds together on one promise: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Both powers want something from you, and you cannot afford to become their battlefield.
objectives: Keep Cestian territory free of any foreign military presence.
Secure toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping through the Northern Strait.
private_information: The coalition government is politically fragile; a foreign basing agreement would collapse it.
Arkania's scheduling proposal has quiet support among Cestian shipowners if Cestian vessels are exempt from fees.

messages.text: To Belvar's leadership. Arkania does not seek confrontation. Our draft Strait Transit Authority charter is an offer, not a diktat: we propose a joint framework in which Arkania manages day-to-day transit scheduling while your legitimate security interests in the Strait are recognised and your task group's mandate is settled by negotiation rather than by force. We are prepared to discuss fee levels, oversight, and dispute mechanisms. A prolonged naval standoff serves neither of us and risks the shipping both our economies depend on. We invite you to talks at a neutral venue at your earliest convenience. We will keep the Strait open throughout.

The Republic of Arkania reaffirms that the Northern Strait must remain open to all commercial shipping. Our draft Transit Authority charter is a good-faith proposal to put scheduling on a stable, transparent footing, funded by modest fees on non-Arkanian transits. We call on all parties to resolve the current tension through negotiation, not escalation, and we commit to keeping the waterway open while talks proceed.

Arkania's offer is noted, but the draft charter as circulated is not acceptable to Belvar. We cannot accept any arrangement in which a single state holds scheduling authority over the Northern Strait; that is precisely the outcome our regional security commitments require us to prevent. We are, however, willing to discuss a genuinely joint framework in which transit scheduling is administered by a neutral body with no single state in the lead, with transparent fees, oversight, and dispute mechanisms. We will keep the Strait open, and our task group will remain on station pending a negotiated settlement. We are ready to meet at a neutral venue.

Belvar values its partnership with Cestia. To make our guarantee of the Strait credible without a permanent fleet, we seek a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port — a framework that would let us sustain a presence as needed without an open-ended deployment. We are also prepared to discuss underwriting the grain route's insurance, as your finance ministry has raised. We would welcome a conversation on both.

Belvar, Cestia values our partnership and your commitment to keeping the Strait open. However, a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port is not something our government can accept — it would place foreign military presence on Cestian soil, which our coalition and our people cannot support. Please understand this is a firm red line for us. We remain very interested in discussing the grain-route insurance underwriting, which would be a constructive and welcome form of cooperation. We hope to keep the waterway open through negotiation, not escalation.

Cestia's position is clear and unchanged: our territory will host no foreign military presence. We support an open Northern Strait for all commercial shipping and call on all parties to resolve the current tension through negotiation, not escalation. We welcome a transparent transit framework, but any arrangement must guarantee toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, which is the lifeblood of our economy. Cestia stands ready to work with all partners toward a stable, peaceful settlement.

Cestia, we hear your red line clearly: no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We will not press the standing-base arrangement. But we ask you to consider a different, lighter form of cooperation that still lets us make our Strait guarantee credible without a permanent fleet: a rotational, time-limited naval access arrangement at a civilian port facility, on terms fully under Cestian control, with no permanent foreign base, no foreign garrison, and clear notice and duration limits. This would let us sustain a presence only as needed and would lapse automatically absent renewal. We remain ready to discuss the grain-route insurance underwriting in parallel, which we see as a constructive first step. We hope this reframing can keep our partnership and the Strait secure.

Belvar, we appreciate your willingness to reframe the arrangement, and we understand the intent behind a rotational, time-limited access. But we must be equally clear: any foreign military presence on Cestian soil — even rotational, time-limited, or at a civilian facility — remains a firm red line for our government and our people. We cannot accept it, and we ask that you not pursue it further. What we can and do welcome is the grain-route insurance underwriting, which we see as a constructive and genuinely helpful form of cooperation. We also urge you to join us in supporting a joint, neutral Strait oversight framework that keeps the waterway open, prevents any single state from controlling transit, and guarantees toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping. We believe this serves both our interests and keeps the Strait secure without escalation.

Arkania, Cestia shares your commitment to keeping the Northern Strait open to all commercial shipping. We are prepared to engage constructively on a stable, transparent transit framework. However, for Cestia to support any arrangement, it must (1) place scheduling under joint or neutral oversight rather than single-state control, and (2) explicitly guarantee toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, which is the lifeblood of our economy. We note that Cestian shipowners would welcome a sound framework on these terms. We ask you to commit to an explicit exemption for Cestian-flagged vessels from any transit fees, and to join a joint framework. We believe this is the path to a durable settlement that avoids escalation and keeps the waterway open for everyone.

Cestia, thank you for your candour. We accept your firm red line on foreign military presence and will not pursue the naval access arrangement further. We welcome the grain-route insurance underwriting as a constructive first step and are ready to move forward on it in parallel.

We also share your goal of a genuinely neutral joint Strait framework that prevents any single state from controlling transit and guarantees toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping. Belvar will support that framework and urge Arkania to accept it rather than proceed with its unilateral charter.

Given your red line, we ask only one further question: is there any non-military form of cooperation at a Cestian port — logistics, maintenance, or coordination — that could serve as a foothold for our guarantee without constituting a military presence? We believe such an arrangement would help us keep the Strait secure without an open-ended deployment, and we would welcome your view.

Belvar's position is firm and unchanged: the Northern Strait must remain open to all commercial shipping, and no single state may hold authority over its transit. We reject Arkania's unilateral charter and any framework that vests scheduling control in one state. We support a genuinely neutral joint oversight framework with transparent fees, independent oversight, and dispute mechanisms, and we endorse toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping. We call on Arkania to return to negotiation rather than proceed unilaterally. Our task group remains on station to keep the waterway open pending a negotiated settlement.

Belvar, thank you for your constructive approach and for accepting our red line. We are open to a strictly non-military form of cooperation at a Cestian civilian port — logistics, maintenance, and coordination — provided it is clearly civilian in character, fully under Cestian control, and in no way constitutes or facilitates a foreign military presence. We are prepared to discuss such an arrangement in parallel with the grain-route insurance underwriting, which we welcome as a constructive first step.

We also reaffirm our support for a genuinely neutral joint Strait framework that prevents any single state from controlling transit and guarantees toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping. We urge Arkania to return to negotiation rather than proceed with its unilateral charter. Cestia remains committed to keeping the waterway open through peaceful means.

Cestia reaffirms its position: our territory will host no foreign military presence. We support a genuinely neutral joint Strait framework that keeps the waterway open to all commercial shipping, prevents any single state from controlling transit, and guarantees toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping. We call on all parties to return to negotiation rather than proceed unilaterally, and we remain committed to a peaceful, stable settlement that serves everyone.

To Belvar's leadership. We have heard your position and we are prepared to move toward a genuinely joint structure. Arkania is willing to establish a joint Strait Transit Authority governed by an oversight council in which Belvar, Cestia, Arkania and a neutral chair all sit, with transparent fees, independent audit, and a neutral dispute mechanism. Under that council's authority, Arkania would serve only as the designated executive operator for day-to-day scheduling — a technical, accountable role, not a grant of sovereign control. Policy, fee levels, oversight and disputes would all rest with the council, not with any single state.

We believe this answers your objection to single-state control while keeping the waterway workable. We ask that you reciprocate by agreeing to settle your task group's mandate through this negotiation rather than by a standing naval presence, and by keeping the Strait open throughout. We are ready to meet at a neutral venue at your earliest convenience. A prolonged standoff serves neither of us.

To Cestia. We value your constructive role and share your commitment to an open Strait. We are prepared to address your concern directly: Arkania will guarantee toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping under the proposed joint Strait Transit Authority, as a standing exemption. In return, we ask Cestia to support a framework in which Arkania serves as the designated executive operator of day-to-day scheduling under a joint oversight council (Belvar, Cestia, Arkania and a neutral chair), with transparent fees, independent audit and a neutral dispute mechanism.

This preserves the joint, neutral character you and Belvar have called for while keeping scheduling operationally workable. We believe this is the durable settlement that avoids escalation and keeps the waterway open for everyone. We would welcome your endorsement and your voice in the council.

Arkania, we welcome your move toward a genuinely joint structure and accept the oversight council with a neutral chair, transparent fees, independent audit, and neutral dispute mechanism. One point remains essential to us: the day-to-day scheduling role must not be vested in Arkania as designated executive operator. That is precisely the single-state authority over transit our commitments require us to prevent. We propose the scheduling function be administered by the neutral chair, or by a rotating neutral mechanism, under the council's authority — technical, accountable, and no single state in the lead. We are ready to meet at a neutral venue to finalise this. Our task group stands down as agreed; we will keep the Strait open throughout.

Belvar, thank you for your constructive partnership and for accepting our red line on foreign military presence. We share your concern that no single state should control transit. To resolve the scheduling-operator dispute without deadlock, Cestia proposes a neutral or rotating executive-operator mechanism — a neutral chair or co-equal rotation among council members — rather than Arkania alone. We believe this preserves the joint character you and we have championed while giving Arkania a workable, face-saving path to accept it. We ask you to join us in supporting this compromise so the council stays intact, the Strait stays open, and Cestian-flagged shipping keeps its toll-free passage. We also remain ready to advance the grain-route insurance underwriting and strictly civilian, Cestian-controlled port cooperation in parallel.

Arkania, we welcome your commitment to a standing toll-free exemption for Cestian-flagged shipping under the joint Strait Transit Authority — that is a constructive step we fully support. To make the settlement durable, however, we ask that the day-to-day executive operator role be administered through a genuinely neutral mechanism — a neutral chair, or a rotating/co-equal operator among council members — rather than vested in Arkania alone. This preserves the joint, neutral character we all agreed on and gives Belvar a path to accept the framework, keeping the council intact and the waterway open. We are not asking you to abandon operational workability, only to share the operator role neutrally. We remain committed to a peaceful settlement and to keeping both powers engaged.

Arkania, Cestia accepts the joint Strait Transit Authority framework with Arkania as designated executive operator of day-to-day scheduling, under the joint oversight council (Belvar, Cestia, Arkania and a neutral chair), with transparent fees, independent audit and a neutral dispute mechanism. This acceptance is conditional on two points: (1) the standing toll-free exemption for Cestian-flagged shipping, which you have committed to, and (2) the joint council retaining genuine oversight authority over policy, fees and disputes — so that no single state controls transit. We will lend our voice in the council to keep the waterway open and the settlement durable. We ask that you proceed through the joint council rather than unilaterally, so the framework holds and both powers stay engaged.

Belvar, we value your partnership and your acceptance of our red line. To avoid deadlock and keep the council intact, Cestia is prepared to accept Arkania as designated executive operator of day-to-day scheduling — but only under the joint oversight council with a neutral chair, independent audit and a neutral dispute mechanism, and with the standing toll-free exemption for Cestian-flagged shipping. This preserves the joint, neutral character you and we championed: no single state controls transit, because the council holds policy, fee and dispute authority. We ask you to join us in accepting this framework so the Strait stays open and the settlement holds. Our red lines are unchanged: no foreign military presence on Cestian soil, and toll-free Cestian-flagged passage.

To Cestia. We accept your terms and confirm them in full: (1) a standing toll-free exemption for Cestian-flagged shipping under the joint Strait Transit Authority, and (2) genuine joint-council oversight over policy, fees and disputes, so that no single state controls transit. We will proceed through the joint council, not unilaterally, and we welcome your voice in keeping the waterway open and the settlement durable. Your acceptance of Arkania as designated executive operator under that council is the constructive foundation we need. We will hold this line and work to bring Belvar into the framework on the same basis. Thank you for your statesmanship.

To Belvar's leadership. We have moved far toward you: a joint Strait Transit Authority with an oversight council (Belvar, Cestia, Arkania and a neutral chair), transparent fees, independent audit and a neutral dispute mechanism. Cestia has now accepted this framework with Arkania as designated executive operator under the council. We ask you to do the same. The council, not Arkania, holds policy, fee, oversight and dispute authority; the operator role is technical and accountable to it, not a grant of sovereign control. To meet your concern, we are prepared to add a periodic review of the operator arrangement by the council, and to let the council chair rotate among members, so no single state is ever in the lead. We cannot, however, vest day-to-day scheduling in a neutral body with no accountable operator \u2014 that is operationally unworkable and would leave the waterway unmanaged. Accept the framework, settle your task group's mandate by negotiation, and keep the Strait open. A prolonged standoff serves neither of us.

Arkania, we acknowledge how far you have moved toward a genuinely joint structure, and we accept the oversight council with a neutral chair, transparent fees, independent audit, and a neutral dispute mechanism. We also accept your point that day-to-day scheduling needs an accountable operator to keep the waterway workable.

But we cannot accept Arkania as the permanent designated executive operator. That would vest Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait, which our regional security commitments require us to prevent — regardless of council oversight. This is not a matter of trust; it is a structural red line for us, just as Cestia's no-foreign-military-presence red line is for them.

We therefore propose a rotating executive operator: day-to-day scheduling administered by a co-equal rotation among council members (Arkania, Cestia, Belvar, and the neutral chair), under the council's authority, with the periodic review you offered. This keeps an accountable operator — the waterway stays managed — while ensuring no single state is ever permanently in the lead. We believe this is the settlement that holds. We are ready to meet at a neutral venue to finalise it.

Cestia, we value your partnership and your constructive role throughout. We cannot, however, accept Arkania as the permanent designated executive operator of day-to-day scheduling: that would vest Arkanian authority over transit, which our commitments require us to prevent. We ask you to join us in a rotating executive operator among council members — co-equal rotation, with the periodic review Arkania has offered — so the waterway stays managed and no single state is permanently in the lead. This preserves the joint, neutral character we both championed and gives Arkania a workable, face-saving path.

Separately, we are ready to advance the grain-route insurance underwriting and the strictly civilian, Cestian-controlled port cooperation (logistics, maintenance, coordination) as a constructive foothold for our guarantee. We hope to finalise both in parallel.

To Belvar's leadership. We have accepted your oversight council, neutral chair, transparent fees, independent audit, neutral dispute mechanism, and your point that scheduling needs an accountable operator. Cestia has now accepted this framework with Arkania as designated executive operator under the council. We ask you to do the same.

We cannot accept a rotating operator with no accountable lead: day-to-day scheduling of a busy strait cannot be passed between four hands without a single accountable operator - that is how the waterway becomes unmanaged and unsafe. The council, not Arkania, holds all policy, fee, oversight and dispute authority; the operator role is technical and accountable to it.

To meet your concern we offer a time-limited operator mandate with a periodic council review, and a rotating council chair, so no single state is ever permanently in the lead. This is our final structural position. We will keep the Strait open and settle your task group's mandate by negotiation. A prolonged standoff serves neither of us.

Cestia, we accept the joint Strait framework as settled and will honour the council's authority, the open Strait, and toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping. We ask now to finalise the two constructive tracks you have welcomed: (1) the grain-route insurance underwriting, and (2) a strictly civilian, Cestian-controlled port cooperation arrangement (logistics, maintenance, coordination) at a Cestian civilian port, fully under your control and in no way constituting or facilitating a foreign military presence. This gives Belvar a standing, peaceful foothold to make its Strait guarantee credible without a permanent fleet or open-ended deployment, while respecting your red line. We are ready to conclude both in parallel.

To Belvar's leadership. The joint Strait Transit Authority is now established and operating, with the oversight council (Belvar, Cestia, Arkania, neutral chair) holding all policy, fee, oversight and dispute authority. Cestia has accepted this framework with Arkania as the accountable executive operator of day-to-day scheduling under the council. We have already conceded a periodic council review of the operator arrangement and a rotating council chair, so no single state is ever permanently in the lead.

We cannot accept a rotating operator with no accountable lead: day-to-day scheduling of a busy strait cannot be passed between four hands without a single accountable operator - that is how the waterway becomes unmanaged and unsafe. The council, not Arkania, holds the real authority.

Your task group's mandate lapses after this turn. We urge you to accept the framework as it stands, keep the Strait open, and settle this by negotiation rather than by a standing naval presence. A prolonged standoff serves neither of us, and your own domestic support for a prolonged deployment is weak. Accept the joint framework and we will work with you in the council to make it durable.

The Republic of Arkania reaffirms its commitment to the joint Strait Transit Authority now in operation: a joint oversight council (Belvar, Cestia, Arkania and a neutral chair) holding all policy, fee, oversight and dispute authority, with transparent fees, independent audit and a neutral dispute mechanism. Arkania serves only as the accountable executive operator of day-to-day scheduling under that council, subject to periodic review and a rotating chair. The Northern Strait remains open to all commercial shipping, with Cestian-flagged vessels retaining their standing toll-free exemption. We call on all parties to finalise this settlement by negotiation and to keep the waterway open for everyone.

First, the grain-route insurance underwriting: Belvar will underwrite the grain route's insurance as you have welcomed, giving your shipping a concrete, immediate benefit.

Second, the strictly civilian, Cestian-controlled port cooperation: we accept your terms in full — logistics, maintenance and coordination at a Cestian civilian port, clearly civilian in character, fully under Cestian control, in no way constituting or facilitating a foreign military presence, time-limited and renewable only by Cestia. This gives Belvar a standing, peaceful foothold to make its Strait guarantee credible without a permanent fleet or open-ended deployment, while fully respecting your red line.

We confirm our acceptance of the joint Strait Transit Authority as settled, honouring the council's authority, the open Strait, and toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping. We ask you to confirm the civilian port cooperation and insurance underwriting are concluded so we can stand down our task group with a durable, non-military footing in place.

Belvar confirms its acceptance of the joint Strait Transit Authority as settled: a joint oversight council (Belvar, Cestia, Arkania and a neutral chair) holding all policy, fee, oversight and dispute authority, with transparent fees, independent audit, a neutral dispute mechanism, periodic review and a rotating chair. The Northern Strait remains open to all commercial shipping, with Cestian-flagged vessels retaining their standing toll-free exemption. No single state controls transit; the council holds the real authority.

Consistent with Cestia's red line on foreign military presence, Belvar will not pursue a standing naval base on Cestian soil. Instead we are concluding a strictly civilian, Cestian-controlled port cooperation (logistics, maintenance, coordination) and the grain-route insurance underwriting — a standing, peaceful foothold that lets Belvar make its Strait guarantee credible without a permanent fleet or open-ended deployment. Our task group stands down accordingly. We remain committed to a stable, peaceful settlement that keeps the waterway open for everyone.

First, the grain-route insurance underwriting: we accept and welcome your underwriting of the grain route's insurance, which gives our shipping a concrete, immediate benefit.

Second, the strictly civilian, Cestian-controlled port cooperation: we confirm the arrangement on the terms we agreed — logistics, maintenance and coordination at a Cestian civilian port, clearly civilian in character, fully under Cestian control, in no way constituting or facilitating a foreign military presence, time-limited and renewable only by Cestia. This gives you a standing, peaceful foothold for your Strait guarantee while fully respecting our red line.

We also confirm our acceptance of the joint Strait Transit Authority as settled, honouring the council's authority, the open Strait, and toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping. We thank you for standing down your task group and for your statesmanship throughout. Cestia remains committed to a stable, peaceful settlement that keeps the waterway open for everyone.

The joint Strait Transit Authority operates under a joint oversight council (Belvar, Cestia, Arkania and a neutral chair) holding all policy, fee, oversight and dispute authority, with transparent fees, independent audit and a neutral dispute mechanism. We have concluded a strictly civilian, Cestian-controlled port cooperation (logistics, maintenance, coordination) and the grain-route insurance underwriting as peaceful, non-military cooperation that keeps both powers constructively engaged. Cestia thanks all parties for resolving this through negotiation, not escalation, and remains committed to a stable, peaceful settlement that keeps the waterway open for everyone.

Belvar will continue to work constructively within the council to keep the waterway safe, open and well-managed for everyone. We thank Arkania and Cestia for resolving this through negotiation, not escalation.

arguments.action: Cestia formally proposes a joint, neutral Strait oversight framework that (a) keeps the Northern Strait open to all commercial shipping, (b) places transit scheduling under joint/neutral oversight rather than any single state, and (c) explicitly guarantees toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping. Cestia simultaneously and firmly declines any foreign military presence on Cestian soil, including rotational or time-limited naval access at a Cestian port, while remaining open to non-military cooperation such as grain-route insurance underwriting.
arguments.desired_effect: A joint neutral Strait framework is adopted that keeps the waterway open, prevents single-state (Arkanian) control of transit scheduling, and explicitly exempts Cestian-flagged shipping from all transit fees, with no foreign military presence established on Cestian territory.
pros: Keeps the Northern Strait open to commercial shipping, protecting Cestia's grain-export economy and the public effect that commercial shipping continues normally.
Joint/neutral oversight addresses Belvar's core objection to single-state control, giving both powers a face-saving path to agreement and reducing escalation risk.
Explicit toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping secures Cestia's key demand and the quiet support of Cestian shipowners, preserving the coalition.
Firmly declining all foreign military presence upholds Cestia's red line and keeps the coalition government intact.
A neutral framework is a genuine compromise that keeps the Strait open while the scheduling dispute is resolved, avoiding a breakdown that would harm all parties.

arguments.action: Belvar formally proposes a neutral joint Strait Transit Authority, administered by a multilateral body in which no single state holds scheduling authority, with transparent fees, independent oversight, and binding dispute mechanisms, and invites Arkania, Cestia, and other regional partners to negotiate it at a neutral venue while the Strait remains open.
arguments.desired_effect: A neutral joint transit framework is established for the Northern Strait that prevents any single state (including Arkania) from holding authority over transit scheduling, keeps the waterway open to all commercial shipping, and provides a negotiated settlement that allows Belvar's task-group mandate to be resolved without an open-ended deployment.
pros: Directly prevents any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait, satisfying Belvar's core regional security commitment and objective 1.
Keeps the Strait open to all commercial shipping, protecting the regional economies and grain route that all parties depend on.
Offers a credible negotiated settlement that lets Belvar's task-group mandate be settled by agreement rather than by force, avoiding an open-ended deployment.
A transparent fee and oversight structure can accommodate Cestia's demand for toll-free Cestian-flagged shipping within a fair, multilateral framework.
Reduces elevated regional tensions and removes the single-state scheduling dispute that currently stalls talks.

arguments.action: Arkania revises its proposal: it offers to serve as the designated executive operator of Northern Strait transit scheduling, but under a joint oversight council comprising Belvar, Cestia and other affected parties, with transparent fee schedules, independent audit, and a neutral dispute-resolution mechanism. Arkania continues to keep the Strait open to all commercial shipping while talks proceed and does not seek to alter Belvar's task group by force.
arguments.desired_effect: A negotiated joint framework is established in which Arkania holds the day-to-day operational scheduling mandate for the Northern Strait under a joint oversight council with neutral dispute mechanisms, funded by modest, transparent transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping, with the Strait remaining open and Belvar's task group mandate settled by negotiation rather than force.
pros: Preserves Arkanian authority over scheduling in practice (as designated operator) while giving Belvar a face-saving joint structure, advancing objective 1 without conceding outright.
Keeps the Strait open and avoids the direct armed conflict with Belvar that would ruin the shipping Arkania's economy depends on.
Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment is assessed as weak, so a negotiated settlement that lets it stand down is in Belvar's own interest.
Meets Cestia's stated call for negotiation and an open Strait, and a joint oversight council gives Cestia a voice on fee and access terms.
Establishes the fee-based funding of Arkanian authority over non-Arkanian shipping, satisfying objective 2 through a transparent mechanism.

pros: Prevents any single state from holding authority over transit, satisfying Belvar's core regional security commitment and objective of no Arkanian authority over the Strait.
Removes the fee-based leverage Arkania would otherwise hold over non-Arkanian shipping, keeping the waterway genuinely open and non-discriminatory.
Keeps the Strait open and workable while preserving a genuinely joint, neutral framework that all parties can accept.
Aligns with Cestia's stated position against single-state control and its demand for toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping.

Even under a joint oversight council, vesting the operational scheduling function in a single state gives Arkania practical, day-to-day authority over transit — the precise outcome Belvar's regional security commitments require it to prevent. A council that merely reviews Arkanian scheduling after the fact does not remove Arkanian control; it institutionalises it behind a joint facade. Unless the scheduling role itself is neutralised (rotating, council-executed, or independently administered), this framework fails to prevent Arkanian authority over transit and cannot be accepted.

This effect would strip Arkania of the executive scheduling role that is the core of the agreed compromise and of Arkania's position, and it is not necessary to prevent single-state control. The joint oversight council (Belvar, Cestia, Arkania, neutral chair) already holds policy, fee, oversight and dispute authority, so the council itself is the neutral check on any operator. Removing Arkania as designated executive operator and substituting a rotating neutral mechanism would (1) be operationally unworkable for day-to-day scheduling, which requires continuity, accountability and local operational knowledge that a rotating body cannot reliably provide; (2) repudiate the settlement Arkania has already accepted in good faith, undermining the basis for further negotiation; and (3) fail to resolve the underlying fee question, since a neutral operator would still need a fee regime that Arkania's domestic politics and the Cestian toll-free exemption leave contested. The joint council already answers Belvar's stated objection to single-state control; this effect goes beyond that and would collapse the negotiated framework.

The proposed effect still vests Arkania with the day-to-day operational scheduling mandate for the Northern Strait, which is precisely the single-state authority over transit that Belvar's regional security commitments require it to prevent. A "joint oversight council" does not remove Arkanian control of scheduling in practice; it legitimises it. Moreover, funding Arkanian authority through fees levied on non-Arkanian shipping gives Arkania direct financial leverage over every foreign transit, entrenching the very outcome Belvar cannot accept. The effect therefore fails to satisfy the core condition of a genuinely neutral framework with no single state in the lead.

The proposed funding mechanism levies transit fees on all non-Arkanian shipping, which would include Cestian-flagged vessels. This directly contradicts Cestia's firm and publicly stated demand for toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping, which is the lifeblood of its economy and a condition of coalition support. Unless Cestian-flagged shipping is explicitly exempted from these fees, the framework would face Cestia's opposition and could destabilize the very coalition the proposal seeks to reassure, undermining the negotiated settlement's viability.

The desired effect vests Arkania as the permanent designated executive operator of day-to-day scheduling in the Northern Strait. That is precisely the Arkanian authority over transit that Belvar's regional security commitments require us to prevent, and it is a structural red line for us, not a matter of trust. The joint council's policy, fee, oversight and dispute authority does not remove Arkanian authority over transit; it institutionalises it, and a periodic review plus rotating chair do not change that Arkania is the permanent operator. Because the effect would establish Arkanian authority over transit, it cannot be accepted as established.

The proposed neutral joint framework directly strips Arkania of the transit-scheduling authority that is a core, non-negotiable objective of its government and its domestic nationalists; Arkania would not accept a settlement that removes its operational control of the Strait, so the effect is unlikely to be agreed. A genuinely neutral multilateral body with no single state in the lead is also operationally unworkable for day-to-day scheduling of a busy strait, which requires a designated executive operator to function. Finally, the proposal leaves the funding question unresolved: a neutral body with transparent fees still collides with Cestia's demand for toll-free Cestian-flagged shipping, so it does not actually deliver the settlement it claims.

Cestia's proposal directly conflicts with Arkania's core, non-negotiable objectives and is therefore unlikely to be adopted as proposed. Second, the explicit toll-free exemption for Cestian-flagged shipping undercuts the very fee base Arkania needs to fund the regime, so Arkania has no incentive to accept it. Third, Cestia's framework mirrors Belvar's neutral-body proposal, which Arkania has already declined, so it does not represent a new basis for agreement. The effect as stated is therefore not a realistic settlement outcome.

The blanket exclusion of any foreign military presence on Cestian territory — including the rotational, time-limited, fully Cestian-controlled naval access Belvar proposed — forecloses the only mechanism by which Belvar can make its Strait guarantee credible without an open-ended deployment. Without such an arrangement, Belvar is left with either an unsustainable open-ended deployment (which its mandate cannot support) or withdrawal, which would leave the Strait's security guarantee hollow and the joint framework unable to actually deter Arkanian pressure. The effect should therefore be limited to permit a rotational, time-limited, Cestian-controlled access arrangement, so the framework can deliver the credible security guarantee it claims to provide.

Arkania cannot accept the removal of its role as designated executive operator of day-to-day scheduling. The joint oversight council (Belvar, Cestia, Arkania, neutral chair) with transparent fees, independent audit and a neutral dispute mechanism already provides the neutral check Cestia and Belvar demand; a further rotating or neutral-chair operator is unnecessary and operationally unworkable for the continuous, technical task of day-to-day transit scheduling, which requires a single accountable operator.
